meta.title: The Studio — AGENVO
meta.description: Agenvo is an architecture, engineering and interiors practice founded in Zurich in 2008. Meet the people, principles and history behind the work.

hero.title: A practice built on *patience.*
hero.body: We are architects, engineers and interior designers who believe the best buildings are not rushed into existence. They are listened for, tested, and slowly made inevitable.

intro.title: An independent studio, deliberately small.
intro.quote: Agenvo was founded on a simple conviction: that architecture should serve the life inside it long after the photographs have faded.
paragraphs: We started in 2008 with two architects, a borrowed drafting table and a commission for a family house above Lake Zurich. Eighteen years later, the studio has grown to sixty-four people across Zurich and Dubai — but the working method has not changed. Every project still begins with a long conversation, a site visit in bad weather, and a physical model.

Our structure is intentionally integrated. Architects sit beside structural engineers, sustainability specialists and interior designers from the first sketch. This means fewer handoffs, fewer compromises, and a building that behaves as one coherent idea rather than a negotiation between disciplines.

We work across residential, commercial, cultural and hospitality projects, at scales from a single room to a district masterplan. What unites the work is not a signature style but a set of standards: honest materials, generous light, calm proportions, and details that reward a second look.

We are equally comfortable restoring a century-old facade and engineering a forty-storey tower. The common thread is care — for the client's ambition, the craftspeople who execute it, and the city that will live with it.
intro.caption: Model-making workshop, Zurich — where every project begins in the hand before it reaches the screen.

beliefs.title:
Four principles.
No exceptions.
beliefs.body: These are not marketing values. They are the questions we ask in every design review, on every project, at every scale.

items.title: Restraint
items.body: The most powerful move is often the one we remove. We edit relentlessly so that what remains — a stair, a window, a wall — can be experienced fully. Restraint is not minimalism for its own sake; it is clarity earned through iteration.

items.title: Material honesty
items.body: Stone should look like stone. Timber should age like timber. We specify materials for how they will look in twenty years, not how they photograph on opening day, and we detail them so they can be repaired rather than replaced.

items.title: Longevity
items.body: A building is a promise to a place. We design for adaptability, low operational carbon and graceful ageing, testing each scheme against a fifty-year horizon. The greenest building is the one that does not need replacing.

items.title: Collaboration
items.body: We are not authors working alone. Clients, engineers, craftspeople and future occupants all hold knowledge the building needs. Our job is to convene that knowledge early and keep it in the room until the last detail is resolved.

timeline.title:
Eighteen years,
one conversation.
timeline.body: A studio evolves the way a building does — slowly, in layers, with each decision making the next one clearer. These are the moments that shaped how we work.

items.title: Two architects, one table
items.body: Elena Marchetti and Jonas Frei establish Agenvo in a former print workshop in Zurich's Kreis 5. The first commission is a private house in Küsnacht, completed on a modest budget and still unaltered today.

items.title: First international project
items.body: A lakeside pavilion on Lake Como brings the studio into Italy. The project establishes our long-running collaboration with local stonemasons and timber fabricators.

items.title: Engineering brought in-house
items.body: Rather than outsourcing structure, we build a dedicated engineering team. The move halves coordination time on complex projects and gives architects direct access to structural thinking from day one.

items.title: Dubai studio opens
items.body: A second studio opens in Dubai's Design District to serve clients across the Gulf, with a focus on commercial towers, hospitality and large-scale masterplanning.

items.title: Water Pavilion wins the ARIA Prize
items.body: The pavilion is recognised for its cantilevered stone roof and zero-discharge water system. It remains our most-visited built work and a testing ground for low-impact construction.

items.title: Carbon-neutral operations
items.body: Both studios transition to verified carbon-neutral operations. We publish our first project carbon assessments and begin specifying embodied-carbon budgets on every new commission.

items.title: Corporate Tower completes
items.body: Our largest project to date opens in Dubai: 48 storeys, a publicly accessible sky lobby, and a facade that cuts solar gain by 38% against the local baseline.

items.title: Sixty-four people, sixteen countries
items.body: The studio is now employee-owned, with a mandate to remain independent. Current research explores low-carbon concrete, prefabricated stone and the adaptive reuse of post-war office stock.

studioLife.title: Where the work happens
studioLife.body: No corner offices, no closed doors. Models are built in the open, drawings are pinned to walls, and the best ideas usually arrive at the long table.

items.caption: The open studio, Zurich — models, samples and drawings share the same table.
Every scheme is studied in physical model at 1:200 and 1:50.
A working material library, not a showroom — samples are borrowed, scuffed and returned.
Friday reviews are open to everyone, from interns to partners.

leadership.title: The people who hold the line

items.name: Elena Marchetti
items.bio: Trained in Milan and Zurich, Elena leads design across the studio's cultural and residential work. She is a visiting critic at ETH and a stubborn defender of the physical model.

items.name: Jonas Frei
items.bio: Jonas built the studio's engineering practice around a simple question: what is the least structure this idea needs? He leads long-span, timber and adaptive-reuse projects.

items.name: Amara Okafor
items.bio: Amara leads interior architecture and the studio's furniture collaborations. Her work is guided by tactility, daylight and the belief that rooms should be generous before they are beautiful.

meta.title: Services — AGENVO
meta.description: Architecture, structural engineering, interior architecture, masterplanning and sustainability services from Agenvo. An integrated practice from first sketch to final handover.

hero.title:
One practice.
*Every discipline.*
hero.body: Architecture, structure, interiors and sustainability under one roof — so the idea survives contact with reality.

architecture.title: Buildings that belong to their place.
paragraphs: We design from the outside in and the inside out at the same time. Context, climate, daylight and the client's daily life are studied together, so that the plan is not a diagram imposed on a site but a response to it.
Our scope runs from feasibility and concept design through planning approval, technical documentation and construction administration. We remain on site until the last handle is fitted.
points: Residential — private houses, villas and multi-family housing
Commercial — offices, headquarters, retail and mixed-use
Cultural and civic — pavilions, galleries, education
Hospitality — hotels, restaurants and destination resorts

engineering.title: Structure as an idea, not an obstacle.
paragraphs: Our in-house structural and MEP engineers are part of the design conversation from the first meeting. That means fewer surprises, faster decisions, and structures that make the architecture possible rather than merely holding it up.
We specialise in long-span concrete, hybrid timber, and the careful intervention of existing structures. Every scheme is modelled, load-tested in principle, and costed before it leaves the studio.

interiors.title:
Rooms that feel finished
before they are furnished.
interiors.body: Interior architecture is not decoration applied at the end. We design the shell, the light, the joinery and the furniture together, so that every element has a reason to be there and nothing fights for attention.

cards.title: Spatial planning
cards.body: We begin with how a room is used at 7am and at 11pm, then design the plan around those routines. Circulation, storage and sightlines are resolved before a single finish is chosen.

cards.title: Bespoke joinery
cards.body: Kitchens, libraries, wardrobes and staircases are drawn to the millimetre and made by workshops we have worked with for over a decade. Built-in, not bolted on.

cards.title: Light and material
cards.body: We layer daylight, architectural lighting and lamps so a room can shift from bright and social to quiet and intimate. Materials are chosen for how they feel barefoot, not just in photographs.

audience: Private clients who want a home that works as well as it looks. Hoteliers and restaurateurs building an atmosphere that guests remember. Developers who understand that interior quality is what sells the last unit as quickly as the first.
We take on full-scope interiors and focused commissions — a single kitchen, a stair, a suite of rooms — where our involvement can meaningfully raise the whole.

advisory.title: Beyond the building.
advisory.body: Not every client needs a full architectural commission. Sometimes the most useful thing we can do is help you decide what to build, whether to buy a site, or how to make an existing building perform. These services can stand alone or sit alongside a design commission.

items.title: Feasibility & site appraisal
items.body: Before you commit capital, we test what a site can realistically hold: planning constraints, massing options, build cost, and the value of each scenario. You receive a clear recommendation, not a stack of drawings.

items.title: Masterplanning & urban design
items.body: For districts, campuses and mixed-use sites, we establish the public realm, density, movement and phasing that allow individual buildings to be designed well later. We often work alongside landscape architects and transport consultants.

items.title: Sustainability & carbon strategy
items.body: We set embodied and operational carbon budgets at concept stage, then track them through design. Services include lifecycle assessment, retrofit strategy, certification support (LEED, BREEAM, Minergie) and passive-design modelling.

items.title: Adaptive reuse & heritage
items.body: The greenest building is usually the one already standing. We survey, assess and transform existing structures — offices, factories, villas — retaining what has value and inserting what a new use requires, with a light touch.

items.title: Design review & second opinions
items.body: Already working with an architect? We offer independent design reviews for developers, boards and private clients — a candid assessment of the scheme, its risks and the highest-value changes before construction begins.

items.title: Construction oversight
items.body: For clients building with another designer, we can act as the owner's representative on site: reviewing workmanship, chairing site meetings, managing variations and protecting the design intent through to handover.

process.title: From first call to final key
process.body: Most commissions follow the same rhythm. The pace changes with scale, but the sequence of decisions does not.

steps.title: Conversation
steps.body: A no-obligation meeting to understand the site, the ambition and the budget. We will tell you honestly if we are the right studio for the job.

steps.title: Proposal
steps.body: A written scope, fee structure and programme, with the team named. No hidden stages, no vague allowances — you know what you are buying.

steps.title: Design
steps.body: Concept, development and technical design, with regular reviews and a physical model at each key milestone. Decisions are documented as we go.

steps.title: Delivery
steps.body: Tender support, contractor selection, site inspections and handover. We stay engaged until the building is performing as designed.

fees.title: Clear from the start.
fees.body: We do not publish a price list, because no two projects are the same. We do commit to a fixed scope and a transparent fee before work begins, and we never bill for time we did not agree.

items.title: Percentage fee
items.body: For full architectural services, fees are typically a percentage of construction cost, staged against deliverables. This aligns our effort with the scale of the build and is standard practice across the profession.

items.title: Fixed fee
items.body: For well-defined scopes — a feasibility study, a single interior, a design review — we quote a fixed sum. You know the total before we start, and scope changes are agreed in writing.

items.title: Retainer
items.body: For developers and long-term clients, a monthly retainer provides ongoing design advice, site visits and planning support across multiple projects or a phased development.

items.title: What is included
items.body: Every proposal names the team, the deliverables, the number of review meetings and the exclusions. Travel, printing and specialist consultants are itemised separately so there are no surprises at invoice stage.

faq.title: Before you write.
faq.body: A few things clients ask us most often. If your question is not here, ask it directly — we answer every enquiry personally.

items.question: Do you work outside Switzerland and the UAE?
items.answer: Yes. We have built in sixteen countries across Europe, the Middle East and Asia. For projects further afield we usually partner with a local architect of record while retaining design leadership, which keeps the process smooth across regulatory systems.

items.question: What size projects do you take on?
items.answer: Our work ranges from a single room or staircase to masterplans of several hundred thousand square metres. What matters is not the size but whether the project offers a genuine design question and a client who wants to engage with it.

items.question: How early should we contact you?
items.answer: As early as possible — ideally before you have purchased a site. A feasibility conversation can save significant cost and heartache later. That said, we regularly join projects at planning stage or even on site, and we are comfortable taking over an existing design.

items.question: Can you work with our existing architect or contractor?
items.answer: Frequently. We provide design review, engineering, interiors or sustainability input to projects led by others, and we are happy to work alongside your contractor from the outset. Clear roles and a written scope keep these collaborations productive.

items.question: How do you approach sustainability?
items.answer: As a design constraint, not an add-on. We set carbon budgets early, prioritise retention and low-carbon materials, model daylight and energy performance throughout, and report actual performance after occupancy. We are happy to work to LEED, BREEAM, Minergie or a bespoke standard.

items.question: Do you take on interior-only projects?
items.answer: Yes. Interior architecture is a full service in its own right, led by Amara Okafor. We take on complete homes, hospitality interiors, and focused commissions such as kitchens, libraries or a single floor of a workplace.

cta.title: A short conversation is usually enough to know.
cta.body: Tell us about the site, the brief, or the problem you are trying to solve. We will respond within two working days with an honest view and a suggested next step.

Built to be
*lived in.*

featured.title: Corporate Tower
featured.body: A 48-storey headquarters designed around a simple move: lift the public life of the building into the sky. A three-level sky lobby, planted terraces on every sixth floor and a facade that shades itself without looking defensive.

items.title: Water Pavilion
items.body: A cantilevered stone roof, a reflecting pool, and a building that almost disappears into the lake.

items.title: Forest Retreat
items.body: Three timber volumes stepped into a slope, each opening to a different horizon. Heated entirely by ground source.

items.title: Skyline Residence
items.body: A tropical villa organised around a shaded courtyard, with deep eaves and cross-ventilation instead of air conditioning.

items.title: Marina Complex
items.body: Three towers on a shared podium, arranged to preserve views and shade a new public waterfront promenade.

items.title: Kant Garagen
items.body: A 1960s car park transformed into studios and workshops, keeping 82% of the original concrete structure.

items.title: Casa Luce
items.body: Our founding commission, revisited: a family house that has aged with its owners and remains unaltered eighteen years on.

items.title: Atelier Nord
items.body: A workplace for a design-led manufacturer, built around a timber-framed central street and a public ground-floor canteen.

items.title: Villa Selva
items.body: A twelve-room hotel in a restored stone farmhouse, with new interventions kept deliberately quiet and reversible.

items.title: Tide House
items.body: A low, single-storey house on sandy ground, raised on timber piles and clad in weathered pine that will silver with the salt air.

caseStudies.title:
A roof that floats,
a floor that reflects.
caseStudies.intro: Lake Como, Italy. A cultural pavilion for a private foundation, open to the public for six months of the year. The brief asked for a room for concerts, readings and silence — and a building that would not compete with the lake.

blocks.title: The challenge
blocks.body: The site sits on a narrow strip between a protected shoreline and a working road. Construction access was limited to a single six-metre gate, and nothing could be built in the lake itself.

blocks.title: The move
blocks.body: We lifted the main volume onto four stone piers, allowing the lake to be seen beneath the building and the ground plane to remain public. The roof cantilevers eight metres, held by a post-tensioned stone beam.

blocks.title: The result
blocks.body: A column-free room for 180 people, naturally lit from above, with a shallow reflecting pool that cools incoming air. The pavilion operates off-grid for water and harvests rainwater from the roof.

caseStudies.title:
Three volumes,
one slope.
caseStudies.intro: A family house in the Swiss Alps, designed for two generations to share without living in each other's pockets. Three timber volumes step down the slope, connected by a glazed spine that becomes the life of the house in winter.
body: The upper volume holds the living spaces and a long terrace facing the valley. The middle volume contains the bedrooms, set back behind a timber screen for privacy. The lowest volume is a self-contained apartment for visiting family, with its own entrance and kitchen.

All three volumes share the same spruce structure, exposed internally and charred externally. The roof is planted with local sedum, and the house draws all its heat from a ground-source loop buried beneath the meadow.

caseStudies.title:
The building was
already there.
caseStudies.intro: A 1960s multi-storey car park in Zurich, due for demolition. We argued for retention — and turned it into forty studios, a workshop, a bakery and a rooftop garden, keeping 82% of the original concrete frame.

quote.text: "Agenvo showed us that the most sustainable building on the site was the one we were about to knock down. That argument changed the entire project."
quote.author: Martin Keller — Development Director, Kant Immobilien

What eighteen years

clients.body: Private families, family offices, developers and cultural institutions. Many have worked with us for more than a decade.

meta.title: Profile — AGENVO
meta.description: Meet the partners, associates and studio team at Agenvo — sixty-four architects, engineers and designers working from Zurich and Dubai.

hero.title:
Sixty-four people.
*One standard.*
hero.body: Architects, engineers, interior designers, model-makers and researchers — working across two studios, one shared table.

partners.title:
The ones who sign
the drawings.
partners.body: Agenvo is employee-owned and led by four partners. Each remains directly involved in projects — reviewing drawings, visiting sites, and sitting in the room when difficult decisions are made. There is no layer between the client and the people doing the work.

items.name: Elena Marchetti
items.bio: Trained in Milan and at ETH Zurich. Elena leads the studio's cultural and residential work, and is responsible for design quality across every commission. She is a visiting critic at ETH and a vocal defender of drawing by hand.

items.name: Jonas Frei
items.bio: A structural engineer who thinks like an architect. Jonas built the in-house engineering team and leads long-span, timber and adaptive-reuse projects. He is the person who asks whether a column can simply disappear.

items.name: Amara Okafor
items.bio: Amara leads interior architecture, material research and the studio's furniture collaborations. Her work is guided by tactility, daylight and the conviction that a room should be generous before it is beautiful. Previously at David Chipperfield Architects.

items.name: Rafael Costa
items.bio: Rafael runs the Dubai studio and the practice's delivery group. He has overseen more than forty completed projects across the Gulf, and is known for protecting design intent through the least glamorous phases of construction.

associates.title: The next generation
associates.body: Associates lead projects day to day and sit on the studio's design review. Several have been with Agenvo for more than a decade.

items.name: Sofia Lindqvist
items.bio: Leads residential and hospitality projects. Joined 2013 from Stockholm.

items.name: Tobias Meier
items.bio: Timber and long-span specialist. Teaches at FH Graubünden.

items.name: Lena Haddad
items.bio: Runs commercial and mixed-use projects across the Gulf. Joined 2016.

items.name: Marco Bianchi
items.bio: Leads furniture and joinery design. Runs the material library.

departments.title:
Four groups,
no silos.
departments.body: Project teams are assembled around the needs of the brief, not the org chart. An architect, engineer and interior designer are assigned to every project from day one, supported by the specialist groups below.

items.title: Design studio
items.body: Architects and urban designers working across all sectors. Responsible for concept, planning and the drawings that define the building. Every project has a named design lead who stays with it from first sketch to handover.

items.title: Engineering
items.body: Structural, facade and building-services engineers. They sit in the same room as the architects and are involved from feasibility onward, so structural logic informs the design rather than arriving after it.

items.title: Interiors
items.body: Interior architects, furniture designers and a full-time material researcher. They work alongside the design team from concept stage and lead the studio's collaborations with craftspeople and manufacturers.

items.title: Delivery & research
items.body: Site architects, technical coordinators and a small research group working on low-carbon concrete, prefabricated stone and adaptive reuse. Research findings feed directly into live projects rather than sitting in a drawer.

culture.title:
A studio that
makes room.
culture.body: We work hard, but we do not mistake hours for output. The studio is set up to protect concentration, encourage argument, and let people have a life outside the building.

items.title: Protected Fridays
items.body: Friday afternoons are reserved for studio-wide reviews, research and model-making. No client meetings, no deadlines. It is where much of our best thinking happens.

items.title: Employee ownership
items.body: Since 2023 the studio has been majority employee-owned. Everyone who has been with us for three years receives a stake, and the partners are accountable to the whole studio.

items.title: Learning budget
items.body: Every person has an annual budget for courses, conferences and travel. We also fund one research sabbatical each year, open to anyone in the studio regardless of seniority.

items.title: Parental support
items.body: Six months of fully paid parental leave for all parents, with a phased return and no expectation of evening calls. Several of our project leads work four-day weeks.

items.title: Studio exchange
items.body: Every year, four people swap between Zurich and Dubai for a month. It keeps the two studios genuinely one practice, and gives younger staff international site experience.

items.title: Make things
items.body: The workshop is open to everyone, not just model-makers. Furniture prototypes, material tests and the occasional wonky chair come out of it. We believe designing is inseparable from making.

careers.title:
Come and
build with us.
careers.body: We are always interested in meeting thoughtful architects, engineers and designers — whether or not there is a role advertised. Send a portfolio and a short note about what you want to learn.

cta.title: You will be working with the people you meet.
cta.body: No account managers, no handoffs to a junior team. The partner you meet at the first conversation will still be reviewing the drawings at handover.

faq.title:
Good to know
before we meet.
faq.body: A short list of the things people most often ask before a first conversation. If yours is not here, just ask.
faq.noteBody: We welcome visitors by appointment, Monday to Friday. Please email the studio at least two days ahead so we can make sure the right people are in.

items.question: How quickly will I hear back?
items.answer: Within two working days, always. If your enquiry is urgent — a planning deadline, a site acquisition, a problem on site — say so in the subject line and we will prioritise it.

items.question: Do you charge for a first meeting?
items.answer: No. The first conversation, whether in the studio or on site, is free and without obligation. We only charge once there is an agreed scope and a signed proposal.

items.question: What should I bring to the first meeting?
items.answer: Whatever you have. A site address, a survey, a mood board, a rough budget or simply a description of how you want to live or work. Drawings are helpful but never required — many of our best projects started with a conversation and a walk around the site.

items.question: Can we visit the studio?
items.answer: Yes. We prefer to meet clients in person, surrounded by drawings and models. Email the studio to arrange a time, and let us know if you would like to see a particular project — we can usually arrange a visit to a completed building too.

items.question: Do you work with clients remotely?
items.answer: Frequently. Roughly a third of our current projects are outside Switzerland and the UAE, and we run them with a mix of video reviews, shared models and regular site visits. For projects far from either studio we usually partner with a local architect of record.

items.question: How do I send drawings or large files?
items.answer: Email us first and we will send a secure upload link. Please do not send large attachments unprompted — they often fail silently. For initial conversations, a few low-resolution images or a PDF under 10 MB is plenty.
